data.q: For navigation calculations, what is the Earth’s approximate compression?
data.e: The working compression is about 0.3 per cent, which is approximately 1 in 300; Bali gives the more exact ratio near 1 in 297.

data.q: What does the term graticule describe?
o: Every line printed on a chart
The network of meridians and parallels on a globe, map or chart
Only the small circles near a pole
data.e: The graticule is the network formed by meridians and parallels, including the prime meridian and equator as its reference lines.

data.q: A great circle has its northern vertex at 70 degrees N, 130 degrees E. Where is the southern vertex?
data.e: Opposite vertices are antipodal, so the latitude changes to 70 degrees S and longitude changes by 180 degrees to 050 degrees W.

data.q: Using a semi-major axis of 6378.4 km and compression of 1/297, what is the approximate semi-minor axis?
data.e: The reduction is 6378.4 divided by 297, about 21.5 km, so the semi-minor axis is approximately 6356.9 km.

data.q: Which datum is used for measuring latitude?
data.e: Latitude is the angular distance north or south of the equatorial plane, so the equator is its datum.

data.q: Where is the difference between geocentric and geodetic latitude greatest?
data.e: The difference is greatest near 45 degrees north and south, where it reaches about 11.6 minutes of arc.

data.q: An aircraft moves from 165 degrees W to 103 degrees W. What is the shorter change of longitude?
data.e: The longitudes have the same name, so subtract to obtain 62 degrees; 103 degrees W lies east of 165 degrees W, giving 62 degrees E.

data.q: An aircraft holds compass heading 355 degrees with deviation 2 degrees west and variation 6 degrees east. What is the true heading?
data.e: Compass plus deviation gives magnetic: 355 minus 2 is 353 degrees M. Magnetic plus easterly variation gives true: 353 plus 6 is 359 degrees T.

data.q: True heading is 015 degrees, variation is 9 degrees west and deviation is 3 degrees east. What compass heading should the pilot steer?
data.e: Reverse the chain by subtracting the signed corrections. True minus westerly variation: 015 minus minus 9 is 024 degrees M. Then 024 minus 3 degrees easterly deviation is 021 degrees C.

data.q: What is the reciprocal of a true direction of 353 degrees?
data.e: A reciprocal is 180 degrees away. Subtracting 180 from 353 gives 173 degrees T.

data.q: What latitude resolution is implied by quoting a position to one decimal minute?
data.e: One decimal minute is 0.1 minute of great-circle arc, about 0.1 NM or 185 m along a meridian.

data.q: If a great circle has its southern vertex at 63 degrees S, 170 degrees W, where is its northern vertex?
data.e: The antipodal vertex has the opposite latitude name and a longitude 180 degrees away, giving 63 degrees N, 010 degrees E.

data.q: Which description defines a great circle?
o: Any circle drawn on the Earth's surface
A surface circle whose plane passes through the Earth's centre
A route that keeps a constant direction
data.e: A great circle has the same centre and radius as the Earth because its plane passes through the Earth's centre.

data.q: What is the defining property of a rhumb line?
o: It always passes through both poles
It is always the shortest surface route
It cuts every meridian at the same angle
data.e: A rhumb line cuts every meridian at the same angle, which makes it a line of constant direction.

data.q: A meridian, considered from one pole to the other, is
o: a semi-great circle and a rhumb line
a complete great circle by itself
neither a great circle nor a rhumb line
data.e: A meridian is one half of a great circle and gives a constant north or south direction, so it is also a rhumb line.

data.q: One minute of longitude represents one nautical mile
data.e: One minute of longitude equals one nautical mile only at the Equator, where the parallel is itself a great circle.

data.q: What is the exact ICAO value of one nautical mile?
data.e: The ICAO nautical mile is exactly 1852 metres. The traditional 6080 figure is in feet.

data.q: How many feet are in one statute mile?
data.e: One statute mile is 5280 ft. It must not be confused with the traditional 6080 ft nautical mile.

data.q: An aircraft flies from 72 degrees north, 002 degrees 30 minutes east to 72 degrees north, 177 degrees 30 minutes west by the shortest route. What is its initial true track?
data.e: The points lie on a meridian and anti-meridian. The shorter great-circle route initially goes north over the North Pole, so the initial track is 360 degrees true.

data.q: Relative to the corresponding great circle, a rhumb line between two ordinary points lies
o: on the same path in every case
data.e: The rhumb line lies on the equatorial side of the great circle, which bows towards the nearer pole.

data.q: Two points on the same meridian are at 41 degrees 25 minutes north and 79 degrees 30 minutes north. Their separation is
data.e: The change of latitude is 38 degrees 05 minutes, equal to 2285 minutes of arc and therefore 2285 NM.

data.q: What is the great-circle distance between antipodal points on the spherical navigation model?
data.e: Antipodes are separated by 180 degrees. Multiplying by 60 gives 10 800 NM, half the Earth's 21 600 NM circumference.

data.q: If the convergency between the end meridians is 14 degrees, the conversion angle is
data.e: Conversion angle is half the meridian convergency, so half of 14 degrees is 7 degrees.

data.q: Which statement about parallels of latitude is correct?
o: Every parallel is a great circle
No parallel is a rhumb line
Only the poles are small circles
Every parallel except the Equator is a small circle and a rhumb line
data.e: Every non-equatorial parallel is a small circle, and it is also a rhumb line because it cuts each meridian at 90 degrees.

data.q: In the red and blue pole convention, the Earth behaves as if which polarity lies in the northern magnetic region?
data.e: The northern magnetic region behaves as a blue polarity, which attracts the red north-seeking end of a compass magnet.

data.q: Magnetic variation is the angle between
o: the horizontal and the total magnetic field
data.e: Variation is the horizontal angle between true north and magnetic north at a stated place and time.

data.q: What is the angle of dip at the magnetic equator?
data.e: Dip is 0 degrees at the magnetic equator because the total field is horizontal there.

data.q: Which equation correctly relates total force T, horizontal force H and vertical force Z?
data.e: The three forces form a right triangle, so the correct relationship is T² = H² + Z².

data.q: Which component of the Earth's magnetic field supplies a heading compass with directive force?
data.e: The horizontal component H is the directive force that aligns the compass with the magnetic meridian.

data.q: What does an agonic line join?
data.e: An agonic line is the zero-value isogonal, so it joins places where magnetic variation is zero.

data.q: A line joining places of equal magnetic dip is called
data.e: An isoclinal joins places of equal magnetic dip. Its zero-dip special case is the aclinic line.

data.q: What is the maximum possible magnitude of magnetic dip?
data.e: Dip reaches 90 degrees at a magnetic pole, where the field is vertical.

data.q: If H is 30 microteslas and Z is 40 microteslas, what is T?
data.e: Using T² = H² + Z² gives T = √(900 + 1600) = 50 microteslas.

data.q: Which description best matches secular change?
o: The compass error caused by aircraft electrical equipment
The daily cycle lasting about 24 hours
A sudden receiver failure during a magnetic storm
The slow long-term drift of the Earth's main magnetic field
data.e: Secular change is the slow long-term change of the main field, which moves poles and isogonals over years and decades.

data.q: What does an isogonal join?
data.e: An isogonal joins places of equal magnetic variation for the stated chart epoch.

data.q: Why does a direct-reading magnetic compass become unreliable near a magnetic pole?
data.e: Near a magnetic pole the field is nearly vertical, so the horizontal directive component H approaches zero and cannot establish a dependable heading.

data.q: Compass deviation is the angle between
data.e: Deviation is the angle between magnetic north and compass north, produced by magnetic influences within the aircraft.

data.q: A constant deviation on every heading is normally represented by which coefficient?
data.e: Coefficient A is the constant term and commonly represents a displaced lubber line or detector alignment error.

data.q: On which pair of headings is coefficient B normally corrected?
data.e: Coefficient B has its maximum semicircular effect on east and west headings, so those headings are used for its correction.

data.q: Observed deviations are north +6 degrees and south minus 2 degrees. What is coefficient C?
data.e: C = (deviation north minus deviation south) divided by 2, so C = [6 minus (minus 2)] divided by 2 = +4 degrees.

data.q: Which item is one of the aims of a compass swing?
o: To align true north with grid north
data.e: A compass swing determines deviation, reduces correctable error and records the residual deviation on the aircraft compass card.

data.q: In the northern hemisphere, acceleration on an easterly heading makes a direct compass show an apparent turn towards
data.e: In the northern hemisphere, acceleration on an east or west heading causes an apparent turn towards north.

data.q: What does UNOS mean for a direct compass in the northern hemisphere?
data.e: UNOS means undershoot north and overshoot south when rolling out using a direct magnetic compass in the northern hemisphere.

data.q: At the magnetic equator, an aircraft accelerates on a westerly heading. What dip-induced indication should be expected?
data.e: There is no dip-induced acceleration error at the magnetic equator because the vertical field component and dip are zero.

data.q: A direct compass described as aperiodic is one that
o: has no liquid in its bowl
data.e: Aperiodic, or dead beat, means the disturbed magnet system settles quickly without continuing to oscillate.

data.q: A bubble in the liquid of a direct compass most strongly suggests
data.e: A bubble commonly indicates a leaking seal and can move through the liquid, creating eddies that disturb the magnet assembly.

data.q: Why is a remote magnetic detector commonly installed near a wingtip or fin?
o: To reduce exposure to aircraft magnetic interference
To make the aircraft turn faster
To remove the need for electrical power
data.e: A remote location is chosen because aircraft magnetic and electrical interference is normally smaller there.

data.q: What does a slaved gyro magnetic compass combine?
o: A direct compass with a wind vane
data.e: The flux-valve reference supplies magnetic north-seeking, while the directional gyro supplies a stable short-term heading display.

data.q: What is departure in navigation?
o: The angular difference between two meridians
The east-west distance between meridians along a stated parallel
The shortest great-circle distance between two positions
data.e: Departure is the east-west distance between two meridians measured along a specified parallel of latitude.

data.q: Two meridians differ by 20 degrees at latitude 52 degrees. What is the departure?
data.e: Departure = 1,200 minutes × cos 52 degrees = 738.8 NM, which is about 739 NM.

data.q: At the equator, a change of longitude of one minute corresponds to a departure of
data.e: At the equator cosine latitude is 1, so one minute of longitude gives 1 NM of departure.

data.q: What is the departure between any two meridians measured exactly at a pole?
data.e: All meridians meet at each pole, so their east-west separation and departure are zero.

data.q: At latitude 60 degrees, 600 NM of departure represents what change of longitude?
data.e: Change of longitude = 600 ÷ cos 60 degrees = 1,200 minutes, which is 20 degrees.

data.q: An aircraft flies 165 km east at 60 degrees north. Approximately what change of longitude results?
data.e: 165 km is about 89 NM. Dividing 89 by cos 60 degrees gives 178 minutes, or 2 degrees 58 minutes.

data.q: A longitude difference of 44 degrees 11 minutes gives 2,000 NM departure. What is the latitude?
data.e: Cos latitude = 2,000 ÷ 2,651 = 0.7544, so the latitude is about 41 degrees north or south.

data.q: For the same change of longitude, which statement is correct?
o: Departure is greatest near a pole
Departure changes sign at the equator
data.e: Departure varies with cosine latitude, so its magnitude decreases as a parallel lies farther from the equator.

data.q: An aircraft flies 300 NM east at 45 degrees north, then later 300 NM west at 50 degrees north and returns to its original latitude. Relative to the start, it finishes
data.e: The same distance at 50 degrees spans more longitude than at 45 degrees, so the westward longitude change is greater and the aircraft finishes west.

data.q: A departure of 240 NM at 44 degrees south spans fixed meridians. What is the departure between them at 40 degrees south?
data.e: Departure at 40 = 240 × cos 40 degrees ÷ cos 44 degrees = 255.6 NM, or about 256 NM.

data.q: From 58 degrees 33 minutes north, 174 degrees west, an aircraft flies exactly 6 NM east. What longitude is reached?
data.e: The longitude change is 6 ÷ cos 58 degrees 33 minutes = 11.5 minutes east, giving 173 degrees 48.5 minutes west.

data.q: For a short 120 NM leg on track 060 degrees true, what is the eastward departure component?
data.e: Departure = distance × sin track = 120 × sin 60 degrees = 103.9 NM, which is about 104 NM east.

data.q: Earth convergency is best defined as
o: the distance between two meridians along a parallel
the angle of inclination between selected meridians at a stated latitude
half the difference between two rhumb-line tracks
the angle between true and magnetic north
data.e: Earth convergency is the angle of inclination between two selected meridians measured at a stated latitude.

data.q: Two meridians are 40 degrees apart at latitude 30 degrees north. Their convergency is
data.e: Convergency = 40 × sin 30 degrees = 20 degrees.

data.q: At the equator, the convergency between two meridians is
o: equal to half their longitude difference
data.e: The local directions of the meridians are parallel at the equator, so convergency is zero.

data.q: At either geographic pole, earth convergency between two meridians is
o: equal to the change of longitude
data.e: At a pole the meridians meet, and their included angle equals their change of longitude.

data.q: Positions A and B differ by 12 degrees of longitude and have a mean latitude of 45 degrees north. Approximate convergency is
data.e: Convergency = 12 × sin 45 degrees = 8.5 degrees.

data.q: A great-circle track changes by 5 degrees between points whose mean latitude is 39 degrees. The longitude difference is approximately
data.e: Change of longitude = 5 ÷ sin 39 degrees, which is approximately 8 degrees.

data.q: Conversion angle between a great-circle direction and the matching rhumb-line direction equals
data.e: Conversion angle is exactly one half of earth convergency.

data.q: From 30 degrees north, 020 degrees west to 30 degrees north, 020 degrees east, the rhumb-line track is 090 degrees true. The initial great-circle track is
data.e: Convergency is 20 degrees and conversion angle is 10 degrees, so the eastbound Northern Hemisphere great circle starts on 080 degrees true.

data.q: The initial great-circle track from A to B is 060 degrees true and convergency is 8.5 degrees in an eastbound Northern Hemisphere case. The initial great-circle track from B to A is
data.e: The track at B has increased to 068.5 degrees true; its reciprocal from B to A is 248.5 degrees true.

data.q: Three waypoints lie at 53 degrees north and are spaced by 10 degrees of longitude. Each great-circle leg has a conversion angle near 4 degrees. At the middle waypoint the track command changes by
data.e: The first leg ends near 094 degrees and the next begins near 086 degrees, giving an 8 degree decrease.

data.q: A is at 55 degrees north on the prime meridian and B is at 54 degrees north, 010 degrees east. If the initial great-circle track from A is 100 degrees true, the approximate rhumb-line track is
data.e: Conversion angle is about 4 degrees, so the eastbound Northern Hemisphere rhumb-line track is 104 degrees true.

data.q: A Southern Hemisphere route spans 16 degrees of longitude at a mean latitude of 42.5 degrees south. Approximate earth convergency is
data.e: Convergency = 16 × sin 42.5 degrees = approximately 10.8 degrees.

data.q: Chart scale is the relationship between
o: a chart length and the corresponding Earth distance
data.e: Scale relates a measured chart length to the corresponding distance between the same positions on Earth.

data.q: Which set gives the three common methods of expressing scale?
o: Statement in words, graduated scale line, representative fraction
data.e: Scale is commonly expressed by a word statement, a graduated scale line or a representative fraction.

data.q: If 1 centimetre on a chart represents 5 kilometres on Earth, the RF is
data.e: Five kilometres equals 500,000 centimetres, so the RF is 1:500,000.

data.q: Five centimetres on a chart represents 7 nautical miles. The RF is closest to
data.e: Seven nautical miles is 1,296,400 centimetres; dividing by 5 gives an RF denominator of 259,280.

data.q: Compared with a small-scale chart, a large-scale chart normally has
o: a larger denominator and less detail
a smaller denominator and more detail
the same denominator and more coverage
a larger denominator and more coverage
data.e: A large-scale chart has a numerically larger fraction, therefore a smaller denominator, and it shows more detail over less area.

data.q: On a 1:5,000,000 chart, a line is 1.7 centimetres long. The Earth distance is approximately
data.e: The line represents 85 kilometres, which is approximately 45.9 nautical miles.

data.q: A scale statement says 1 inch represents 10 nautical miles. The representative fraction is approximately
data.e: Ten nautical miles is 10 × 6,080 × 12 = 729,600 inches, giving 1:729,600.

data.q: On a chart with RF 1:1,000,000, what chart length represents 50 kilometres?
data.e: Fifty kilometres is 5,000,000 centimetres; dividing by 1,000,000 gives 5 centimetres.

data.q: On a 1:500,000 chart, the chart length representing 30 kilometres is
data.e: Thirty kilometres is 3,000,000 centimetres; dividing by 500,000 gives 6 centimetres.

data.q: If 3 centimetres on a chart represents 200 statute miles, the RF is closest to
data.e: Converting 200 statute miles to centimetres and dividing by 3 gives a denominator of about 10,728,960.

data.q: At RF 1:2,000,000, a chart line of 4.2 inches represents approximately
data.e: Earth distance = 4.2 × 2.54 × 2,000,000 centimetres = 213.36 kilometres.

data.q: At RF 1:1,000,000, what chart length represents 400 kilometres?
data.e: Four hundred kilometres gives 40 centimetres on the chart, which is approximately 15.74 inches.

data.q: In chart projection, the reduced Earth is
o: the area omitted from a chart
a scale model of the Earth used as the projection basis
the part of the globe below the equator
data.e: The reduced Earth is the scale model of the globe on which the projection is based.

data.q: The three general developable projection surfaces are
data.e: The three general families use a plane, a cylinder or a cone as the developable surface.

data.q: On a polar azimuthal projection, the graticule normally shows
o: straight meridians radiating from the pole and concentric latitude circles
data.e: A polar plane projection has straight radiating meridians and concentric circular parallels.

data.q: A normal cylindrical graticule is characterised by
o: parallel straight meridians and parallel straight latitudes
data.e: The normal cylindrical family opens into parallel straight meridians crossed by parallel straight latitudes.

data.q: A typical conical graticule has
o: parallel meridians and equally spaced latitudes
one meridian and one latitude only
straight meridians converging towards an apex and parallels as circular arcs
data.e: On a conical chart the meridians converge towards the cone apex and the parallels are arcs centred on it.

data.q: Which ideal property cannot remain both constant and correct over an extensive flat chart?
data.e: Constant correct scale over a large flat chart is impossible; it can be exact only at selected points or lines.

data.q: An orthomorphic or conformal chart is one on which
o: local angles and bearings are represented correctly
every great circle and rhumb line is straight
data.e: Conformality preserves local angles, allowing chart bearings to match directions on Earth.

data.q: The first condition for conformality is that
o: meridians and parallels intersect at 90 degrees
data.e: A conformal graticule must preserve the right-angle crossing of meridians and parallels.

data.q: The second condition for conformality requires scale at a point to
o: be equal in every direction or change equally in every direction
remain constant over the whole chart
data.e: At one point, directional scale must match, or change at the same rate in every direction.

data.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes projection construction?
o: All operational charts are direct photographs
All projections must use a physical light source
Non-perspective means the chart has no graticule
Perspective uses geometric rays, while non-perspective construction is mathematical or mathematically modified
data.e: Perspective construction uses projection rays; non-perspective charts are produced or corrected mathematically.

data.q: Which pair belongs to the navigation requirements of an ideal chart?
o: Straight rhumb lines and straight great circles
A single worldwide RF and no graticule
data.e: An ideal navigation chart would show both rhumb lines and great circles as straight lines.

data.q: On a secant conical projection, scale is normally correct along
data.e: A secant cone cuts the reduced Earth along two standard parallels, where scale is correct.

data.q: A normal Mercator chart is correctly described as
data.e: The normal Mercator is cylindrical, mathematically modified and conformal, so it is non-perspective.

data.q: The graticule of a direct Mercator chart is
data.e: Parallel straight meridians and parallel straight latitudes form a rectangular Mercator graticule.

data.q: On a normal Mercator, meridians are
data.e: Mercator meridians are straight parallel lines with equal spacing.

data.q: How are parallels of latitude shown on a normal Mercator?
o: As straight parallel lines whose spacing increases towards the poles
As curves concave to the equator
data.e: Mercator parallels are straight and parallel, with their separation increasing poleward.

data.q: A rhumb line on a Mercator chart is represented by
o: a curve concave to the equator
a curve convex to the equator
a complex curve except at low latitude
data.e: A straight line cuts every parallel Mercator meridian at the same angle, so it is a rhumb line.

data.q: On a direct Mercator, great circles are shown as
o: straight lines for the equator and meridians, but curves for all others
data.e: The equator and meridians are straight great circles; every other great circle appears curved.

data.q: Apart from the equator and meridians, a great circle on Mercator is a curve
o: with no fixed relationship to the equator
data.e: The Mercator great-circle curve is concave to the equator and lies poleward of the corresponding rhumb line.

data.q: Chart convergence on a normal Mercator is
data.e: Mercator meridians are parallel, so their chart convergence is zero everywhere.

data.q: Mercator conformality means that the chart preserves
data.e: A conformal Mercator preserves local angles and therefore locally correct bearings.

data.q: Why can the geographic poles not be shown on a normal Mercator?
o: Scale and latitude spacing become infinite as latitude approaches 90 degrees
The equator blocks the projection rays
data.e: Mercator scale and parallel spacing grow without limit towards 90 degrees, placing the poles at infinity.

data.q: Compared with the equator, Mercator scale at 60 degrees latitude is
data.e: Relative Mercator scale is secant latitude; sec 60 degrees equals 2.

data.q: The rhumb-line track from Turin to Khartoum is 145 degrees true. With a conversion angle of 6 degrees, the initial great-circle track at Turin is
data.e: The Northern Hemisphere south-eastbound great circle starts poleward of the rhumb line, giving 145 minus 6 = 139 degrees true.

data.q: The scale at latitude L on a normal Mercator is
o: equatorial scale multiplied by sec L
equatorial scale multiplied by cos L
equatorial scale divided by tan L
data.e: Mercator scale at latitude L is the equatorial scale multiplied by secant L.

data.q: A Mercator has scale 1:1,000,000 at the equator. Its scale at 60 degrees north is
data.e: Secant 60 degrees is 2, so the scale doubles and the RF becomes 1:500,000.

data.q: The scale at 52 degrees south is 1:2,000,000. The approximate equatorial scale is
data.e: The equatorial denominator is 2,000,000 divided by cos 52 degrees, approximately 3,249,000.

data.q: Moving poleward on a normal Mercator causes
o: scale to contract and the RF denominator to fall
scale to expand and the RF denominator to rise
scale to expand and the RF denominator to fall
data.e: Mercator scale expands poleward, which means the representative-fraction denominator falls.

data.q: The scale is 1:2,000,000 at 54 degrees south. At 25 degrees north it is approximately
data.e: Using the cosine ratio gives a denominator of about 3,083,806, so 1:3,084,000 is correct.

data.q: A short distance on a Mercator chart should be measured against
o: latitude graduations at the mid-latitude of the leg
latitude graduations at the nearest pole
data.e: Use the graduated meridian at the leg's mid-latitude because that represents the appropriate local scale.

data.q: Why must longitude graduations not be used as a general distance scale?
o: One minute of longitude equals one NM only at the equator
data.e: A minute of longitude represents one nautical mile only on the equator, so longitude graduations are not a general distance scale.

data.q: The chart distance between the same two meridians on a normal Mercator
o: is the same at every latitude
data.e: Mercator meridians are parallel and equally spaced, so their chart separation is constant with latitude.

data.q: On a Mercator, 160 east to 160 west measures 30 cm. At 30 degrees south, the scale is approximately
data.e: The 40 degree departure at 30 degrees south is about 2,078 NM, giving an RF of about 1:12,831,000.

data.q: A normal Mercator remains within about 1 percent of equatorial scale to
data.e: The practical one-percent band extends roughly 8 degrees, or about 480 to 500 NM, each side of the equator.

data.q: On a secant Mercator, scale is exactly correct
data.e: A secant Mercator is correct in scale along its two standard parallels.

data.q: Meridians 5 degrees apart measure 8 cm at 60 degrees north. The Mercator scale is nearest
data.e: Five degrees of longitude at 60 degrees is 150 NM; over 8 cm this gives approximately 1:3,472,500, nearest 1:3,500,000.

data.q: The principal navigation advantages sought in a Lambert conformal chart are
o: straight rhumb lines and true area
constant scale at every point and straight meridians
a visible geographic pole and equal area
near constant scale and nearly straight great-circle routes
data.e: Lambert was designed to give near constant scale and make a straight chart line a close approximation to a great circle.

data.q: On a simple conic projection, scale is correct at
data.e: The simple cone touches the reduced Earth at its parallel of tangency, so scale is correct there.

data.q: For a Lambert chart whose parallel of origin is 45 degrees north, the constant of the cone is approximately
data.e: The cone constant is sine 45 degrees, which is approximately 0.707.

data.q: With n equal to 0.707, a change of longitude of 100 degrees gives chart convergence of
data.e: Chart convergence is longitude change multiplied by n, so 100 × 0.707 = 70.7 degrees.

data.q: On a Lambert conformal chart, scale is exactly correct at
data.e: The two circles where the modified cone intersects the reduced Earth are the standard parallels of correct scale.

data.q: How does Lambert scale behave between and outside its standard parallels?
data.e: Lambert scale is contracted between the standard parallels and expanded outside them.

data.q: The parallel of origin on a Lambert chart
o: defines the cone constant and normally lies halfway between the standard parallels
is the only line of correct scale
data.e: The parallel of origin is normally midway between the standard parallels and its sine defines n.

data.q: Under the one-sixth rule, the standard parallels are placed
o: together at the centre of the sheet
at the top and bottom edges
one sixth of the sheet in from the top and bottom
one sixth of a degree apart
data.e: The one-sixth rule places each standard parallel about one sixth of the sheet height in from its nearest edge.

data.q: A Lambert chart has standard parallels at 63 degrees north and 41 degrees north. Its cone constant is nearest
data.e: The parallel of origin is 52 degrees north and sin 52 degrees is approximately 0.788.

data.q: Standard parallels are 41 degrees 20 minutes north and 11 degrees 40 minutes north. The cone constant is nearest
data.e: Their midpoint is 26 degrees 30 minutes north; sin 26 degrees 30 minutes is approximately 0.446.

data.q: Lambert's conformal conic is
data.e: Lambert's chart is a mathematically modified, non-perspective, conformal conic projection.

data.q: Lambert conformal charts are especially suitable for
o: mid-latitude aeronautical route and plotting charts
a single world chart including both poles
data.e: Their conformality, near constant scale and near-straight great circles suit mid-latitude aviation charting.

data.q: For practical aviation use, a chart may be treated as constant scale when its scale distortion does not exceed about
data.e: A Lambert sheet is treated as practically constant scale when its distortion remains within about 1 percent.

data.q: A Lambert chart whose standard parallels are 16 degrees apart has an approximate maximum scale error of
data.e: Oxford's guide gives about 1 percent maximum scale error for 16 degrees of standard-parallel separation.

data.q: The difference between a rhumb-line direction and the corresponding great-circle direction is
data.e: Conversion angle is half Earth convergency and separates the rhumb line from the great circle.

data.q: On Lambert, the difference between a rhumb line and a straight chart line is
data.e: A Lambert straight line differs from the rhumb-line direction by half chart convergence at an endpoint.

data.q: Except at the parallel of origin, a great circle on Lambert appears as
o: a curve concave to the pole
a shallow curve concave to the parallel of origin
a curve concave to the equator in every case
data.e: The Lambert great circle is a shallow curve concave to the parallel of origin.

data.q: Apart from meridians, rhumb lines on a Lambert chart are
o: curves concave to the pole of projection
data.e: Lambert rhumb lines, except meridians, curve concave to the pole of projection.

data.q: At the mid-meridian of a Lambert route, the straight line, great circle and rhumb line are
data.e: The three route representations are parallel at the mid-meridian.

data.q: A Lambert straight line from A to B measures 250 degrees true at A and chart convergence is 6 degrees north. The rhumb-line track is
data.e: Half chart convergence is 3 degrees, so the rhumb line is 250 minus 3 = 247 degrees true.

data.q: Distance on a Lambert chart should normally be measured using
o: longitude graduations at the chart edge
latitude graduations along a suitable meridian
data.e: A graduated meridian supplies the latitude scale, with one minute of latitude representing one nautical mile.

data.q: A true VOR bearing plotted on Lambert should be referenced to
data.e: VOR bearing is established at the ground station, so it is plotted from the station's meridian using variation at the station.

data.q: An aircraft heads 330 degrees true and observes an NDB at relative bearing 090 degrees. The reciprocal position line through the NDB is plotted as
o: 240 degrees from a line parallel to the aircraft's meridian
data.e: The bearing to the NDB is 060 degrees true, so its reciprocal is 240 degrees plotted from a transferred aircraft meridian through the NDB.

data.q: On a Lambert chart n is 0.80. Initial straight-line track is 070 degrees true and rhumb-line track is 082 degrees true. From 4 degrees west, the destination longitude is
data.e: The 12 degree track difference is half chart convergence; full convergence is 24 degrees, giving 30 degrees of longitude and destination 26 degrees east.

data.q: For a North Polar stereographic chart, the plane touches the North Pole and the projection point is at
data.e: A North Polar stereographic is projected from the diametrically opposite South Pole onto a plane tangent at the North Pole.

data.q: The co-latitude of 70 degrees north is
data.e: Co-latitude equals 90 minus latitude, so 90 minus 70 gives 20 degrees.

data.q: Polar stereographic scale away from the pole varies approximately as
o: secant squared of half the co-latitude
data.e: The polar scale factor is sec² of half the co-latitude.

data.q: Polar stereographic scale remains within about 1 percent of polar scale from the pole to
data.e: The scale is within about 1 percent between 90 and 78 degrees latitude.

data.q: On a polar stereographic chart, chart convergence between two meridians equals
data.e: The polar convergence factor n is 1, so chart convergence equals the full longitude difference.

data.q: On a polar stereographic, the initial straight-line track from 75 north 60 west to 75 north 60 east is
data.e: The meridians differ by 120 degrees and form an isosceles polar triangle, leaving a 30 degree initial track angle.

data.q: Grid navigation is used at high latitude mainly because
o: local True North changes rapidly as converging meridians are crossed
data.e: Rapid meridian convergence rotates local True North, while parallel grid lines provide a fixed direction datum.

data.q: On a standard North Polar grid, the convergence at 45 degrees west is
data.e: North Polar standard-grid convergence has the longitude's magnitude and the opposite east or west name, giving 45 degrees east.

data.q: A grid direction of 105 degrees with convergence 20 degrees west converts to true direction
data.e: With west convergence, true is greater than grid, so 105 plus 20 gives 125 degrees true.

data.q: Grivation is the algebraic sum of
data.e: Grivation combines magnetic variation and grid convergence algebraically.

data.q: Grid heading is 090 degrees and grivation is 20 degrees east. The corresponding magnetic heading is
data.e: From Grid to Magnetic, east grivation is subtracted, giving 090 minus 20 = 070 degrees magnetic.

data.q: When a directional gyro is used for grid steering, the normal treatment is to
o: correct transport wander but ignore Earth rate
correct Earth rate but not normal transport wander
ignore both Earth rate and real drift
slave it continuously to Magnetic North
data.e: The gyro is aligned to Grid North and corrected for Earth rate; normal transport-wander correction is not applied because the grid is fixed.

data.q: Which of these chart scales normally gives the greater ground detail?
data.e: The 1:500,000 chart is the larger scale among these choices and normally shows more ground detail.

data.q: On a contour chart, very closely spaced contours indicate
data.e: A steep slope produces a large elevation change over a short horizontal distance, so its contours lie close together.

data.q: A Maximum Elevation Figure shown in a grid square should be treated as
o: terrain and obstacle information, not automatically a safe altitude
data.e: A Maximum Elevation Figure reports the dominant elevation under the chart's stated method; it is not automatically a safe altitude.

data.q: To interpret an airspace boundary correctly, the pilot must read
o: its symbol, label, vertical limits and effective details
data.e: The complete meaning comes from the boundary symbol together with its label, vertical limits and effective details.

data.q: Which feature is normally the most useful precise visual checkpoint?
o: one village among many similar villages
data.e: A large motorway junction is conspicuous, accurately positioned and usually more unique than the other choices.

data.q: Reading map to ground is the normal method when the aircraft is
data.e: When near track and time, map to ground predicts what should appear next and directs the outside search.

data.q: When position is uncertain, ground to map means
o: following a road without identifying it
matching an observed arrangement of features to the chart
data.e: Ground to map starts with a distinctive observed pattern and searches for that same arrangement on the chart.

data.q: At a groundspeed of 150 kt, the aircraft travels how far in 6 minutes?
data.e: Six minutes is one tenth of an hour, so 150 divided by 10 gives 15 NM.

data.q: Two line features crossed approximately at right angles to track are especially useful for
data.e: The known chart distance between transverse line features can be compared with elapsed time to check groundspeed.

data.q: As visual navigation altitude increases, which change is generally expected?
o: all charted masts become easier to see
near hills always hide more of the horizon
a wider pattern is visible but small vertical features lose prominence
data.e: Greater altitude widens the view, while small masts and local vertical relief become less prominent.

data.q: Which factor can substantially change the visual contrast of a checkpoint?
data.e: Season, light and weather can change colour, shadow, water extent and surface appearance.

data.q: Before using a printed aeronautical chart, the pilot should first ensure that
o: its edition and operational information are current
every symbol is memorised without the legend
only the magnetic variation is checked
data.e: The chart edition and operational information must be current through the applicable aeronautical information and NOTAM.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: The measurement of a day is based primarily on Earth's
data.e: A day is defined from Earth's rotation measured against the Sun or a distant star.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: Perihelion normally occurs in
data.e: Earth is nearest the Sun at perihelion in early January.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: Viewed from the North Celestial Pole, Earth moves around the Sun
data.e: Viewed from above the North Celestial Pole, Earth follows its elliptical orbit anticlockwise.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: The principal cause of the seasons is
data.e: The seasons result mainly from the approximately 23.5 degree inclination of Earth's axis from the normal to its orbital plane.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: The angle between the ecliptic and the equinoctial is approximately
data.e: The obliquity of the ecliptic is approximately 23.5 degrees.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: At the Southern Hemisphere winter solstice, the Sun's declination is approximately
data.e: Southern Hemisphere winter occurs near the June solstice, when solar declination is about 23.5 degrees north.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: Compared with an apparent solar day, a sidereal day is
data.e: A sidereal day is about 23 hours 56 minutes, roughly 4 minutes shorter than a mean or typical apparent solar day.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: A mean solar day is
o: one orbit measured against a star
the annual average of apparent solar days
data.e: The mean solar day is the average length of apparent solar days over the year and is fixed at 24 hours.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: The maximum difference between mean time and apparent solar time is about
data.e: Oxford gives the largest equation of time difference as about 16 minutes in mid November.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: The tropical year is approximately
data.e: The tropical year, measured by the seasonal cycle, is about 365 days 5 hours 48.75 minutes.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: Greenwich Hour Angle is measured
o: westwards from Greenwich from 0 to 360 degrees
eastwards from Greenwich from 0 to 180 degrees
data.e: GHA is the equinoctial arc measured westwards from the Greenwich meridian from 0 to 360 degrees.

chapter: Time 1: The Solar System and Time

data.q: A celestial body with GHA 270 degrees is transiting which equivalent geographic meridian?
data.e: A GHA of 270 degrees west is the same meridian as longitude 090 degrees east.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: An arc of 153 degrees 30 minutes is equivalent to approximately
data.e: At 15 degrees per hour, 153 degrees 30 minutes converts to 10 hours 14 minutes.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: To find LMT from UTC at an easterly longitude, the longitude expressed as time is
o: always rounded to a whole hour
data.e: East longitude is ahead of UTC, so its arc time is added to UTC to obtain LMT.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: If it is 0900 LMT at Greenwich, what is the LMT at 045 degrees east?
data.e: Forty five degrees equals 3 hours, and east is later, giving 1200 LMT.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: If Cairo at 030 degrees east has 0900 LMT, the corresponding UTC is
data.e: Thirty degrees equals 2 hours; east LMT is ahead, so 0900 minus 0200 gives 0700 UTC.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: The normal width of a theoretical full time zone is
data.e: Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour, so a theoretical full zone is 15 degrees wide.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: Using Oxford's zone number convention, longitude 137 degrees east lies in zone number
data.e: 137 divided by 15 is 9.13, rounded to 9, and east longitude receives a negative zone number, giving -9.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: The algebraic relationship between UTC, Zone Time and Zone Number is
o: UTC equals Zone Time minus longitude
Zone Time equals UTC plus longitude
UTC equals Zone Time divided by Zone Number
data.e: The governing relationship is UTC = Zone Time + Zone Number.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: Indian Standard Time is
data.e: Indian Standard Time is UTC + 5 hours 30 minutes, based on 82 degrees 30 minutes east.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: Why may a country's Standard Time differ from theoretical Zone Time?
o: Earth rotates at different rates by country
Latitude changes the length of an hour
Legal and administrative boundaries determine Standard Time
UTC is not used in aviation
data.e: Standard Time is a legal and administrative choice, so its boundary need not follow a theoretical 15 degree zone.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: When crossing the International Date Line eastbound, the traveller normally
o: keeps both time and date unchanged
data.e: Eastbound crossing subtracts one calendar day; westbound crossing adds one day.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: A flight leaves 175 degrees east at 0100 LMT on 18 November, flies eastbound for 4 hours, and arrives at 150 degrees west. The arrival LMT is
data.e: Departure converts to 1320 UTC on 17 November; after 4 hours it is 1720 UTC, then minus 10 hours gives 0720 LMT on 17 November.

chapter: Time 2: UTC, Zone Time and the Date Line

data.q: At longitude 130 degrees east, Zone Time is 0600 on 1 January and the zone number is -9. The UTC is
data.e: UTC = 0600 + (-9 hours), which gives 2100 UTC on 31 December.

data.q: On 21 June, the lowest listed northerly latitude at which the Sun remains above the horizon all day is
data.e: The Air Almanac question gives 66 degrees north as the lowest listed latitude with continuous daylight on 21 June.

data.q: On 21 December, the lowest listed northerly latitude at which the Sun does not rise is
data.e: The Air Almanac question gives 68 degrees north as the lowest listed latitude at which the Sun does not rise on 21 December.

data.q: Civil twilight ends in the evening when the centre of the Sun reaches
data.e: Evening civil twilight ends when the Sun's centre is 6 degrees below the sensible horizon.

data.q: Nautical twilight occurs while the Sun's centre is between
o: 6 and 12 degrees below the sensible horizon
data.e: Nautical twilight is the band from 6 to 12 degrees below the sensible horizon.

data.q: Between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south, the minimum civil-twilight duration is about
data.e: The minimum is about 21 minutes at the equator, where the Sun crosses the horizon most steeply.

data.q: Compared with the sea-level table, an observer at high altitude normally sees
o: later sunrise, earlier sunset and longer twilight
earlier sunrise, later sunset and shorter twilight
the same sunrise and sunset with shorter twilight
earlier sunrise, earlier sunset and unchanged twilight
data.e: Greater height produces earlier sunrise, later sunset and generally shorter civil twilight.

data.q: At visible sunrise, the point of the Sun used to define the event is the
o: upper limb first appearing at the visible horizon
lower limb touching the sensible horizon
centre reaching 6 degrees below the horizon
data.e: Visible sunrise is defined by the upper limb first appearing at the visible horizon.

data.q: Air Almanac sunrise and twilight values are normally tabulated as
o: Standard Time for the capital city
zone time for mean sea level
LMT for an observer at sea level
data.e: The tables provide Local Mean Time for the stated latitude and date at sea level.

data.q: For a Delhi sunrise problem, the Air Almanac table is entered initially with
data.e: Date and latitude select the Air Almanac value; longitude is used later to convert LMT to UTC.

data.q: Sunset at New York is 1929 LMT and ECT is 2001 LMT. Evening civil twilight lasts
data.e: Evening civil twilight duration is ECT minus sunset, so 2001 minus 1929 is 32 minutes.

data.q: At visible sunset the centre of the Sun is approximately
o: 50 minutes of arc below the sensible horizon
data.e: Refraction of about 34 minutes plus the Sun's radius of about 16 minutes places its centre roughly 50 minutes below the sensible horizon.

data.q: For two places on the same latitude and date, the Air Almanac sunrise value in LMT is
data.e: Sunrise occurs at the same Local Mean Time along the same parallel on the same date; longitude changes the corresponding UTC.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: The direction in which the longitudinal axis of an aircraft points is its
data.e: Heading is the direction in which the aircraft's longitudinal axis points.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: The direction of the path actually followed over the Earth's surface is the
data.e: Track is the direction of the aircraft's actual path over the Earth's surface.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: An aircraft flies heading 000 degrees and makes good track 010 degrees. Its drift is
data.e: Track lies 10 degrees to the right of heading, so the aircraft has 10 degrees right drift.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: To maintain a required track in a crosswind, the wind correction angle is normally
o: equal to the drift and in the same direction
equal to the drift and in the opposite direction
data.e: The wind correction angle is equal in magnitude and opposite in sense to the drift it prevents.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: A wind reported from 330 degrees is drawn in the triangle of velocities towards
data.e: Wind is reported from 330 degrees but its vector points downwind towards 150 degrees.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: In the usual navigation vector convention, the wind vector is identified by
data.e: The wind vector carries three arrowheads; the air vector carries one and the ground vector carries two.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: For heading 000 degrees, TAS 100 kt and wind 240 degrees at 30 kt, the approximate scale-drawing result is
data.e: The scale drawing gives a track of about 012 degrees and a groundspeed of about 118 kt.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: With a wind exactly at right angles to the required track, the groundspeed after correcting heading is
data.e: Crabbing uses part of the air vector across the track, so a pure crosswind gives a groundspeed less than TAS.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: Required track is 120 degrees, TAS 180 kt and wind is 340 degrees at 50 kt. The approximate heading and groundspeed are
data.e: Opening the triangle gives approximately heading 110 degrees and groundspeed 216 kt.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: True heading is 310 degrees, TAS is 200 kt, groundspeed is 176 kt and drift is 7 degrees right. The approximate wind is
data.e: Opening the known air and ground vectors gives a wind of approximately 270 degrees at 33 kt.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: From a fix, an aircraft flies heading 090 degrees at 120 kt TAS for 30 minutes. Before wind displacement is applied, its air position is
data.e: The air distance is 120 multiplied by 0.5 hour, so the air position is 60 NM east of the fix.

chapter: Dead Reckoning and the Triangle of Velocities

data.q: A complete dead-reckoning plot advances the last confirmed fix by applying
o: direction, speed, time and forecast wind
data.e: A complete DR plot advances the last confirmed fix using direction, speed, elapsed time and the forecast wind.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: Pressure altitude is the altitude indicated when the altimeter subscale is set to
data.e: Pressure altitude is read with the standard pressure setting of 1013.25 hPa on the subscale.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: Calibrated airspeed is obtained by correcting IAS for
data.e: CAS is IAS corrected for position or pressure error; the aircraft card may combine this with instrument correction.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: At FL 200 in ISA, relative density is about 0.533. A CAS of 100 kt gives a TAS closest to
data.e: TAS is 100 divided by the square root of 0.533, which is approximately 137 kt.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: Which sequence correctly follows the airspeed corrections?
data.e: The correct sequence is IAS, CAS, EAS, TAS as position, compressibility and density corrections are applied.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: The difference between total air temperature and static air temperature is called
data.e: Ram rise is the heating difference between TAT and SAT caused by slowing and compressing the airflow at the probe.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: A recovery factor of one means that the temperature probe
o: recovers the full theoretical ram rise
shows SAT directly at every speed
data.e: Recovery factor one represents full recovery of the theoretical ram-temperature rise.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: The local speed of sound in ISA conditions at mean sea level is approximately
data.e: At 288.15 K the local speed of sound is approximately 661 kt.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: At SAT minus 42 degrees Celsius and Mach 0.86, the TAS is closest to
data.e: The local speed of sound is about 593 kt, and 0.86 multiplied by 593 is about 510 kt TAS.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: If TAS remains constant while SAT decreases, Mach number will
data.e: Colder air lowers the local speed of sound, so the same TAS represents a higher Mach number.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: Density altitude is best defined as
o: the ISA altitude having the existing air density
data.e: Density altitude is the altitude in the ISA atmosphere at which the existing density would occur.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: At pressure altitude 5,000 ft and OAT 25 degrees Celsius, the density altitude using Bali's 118 factor is closest to
data.e: ISA temperature is about 5.1 degrees Celsius, giving a positive deviation near 19.9 degrees and density altitude near 7,348 ft.

chapter: TAS, Mach Number and Density Altitude

data.q: The airspeed used as the magnitude of the air vector in the triangle of velocities is
data.e: TAS is the aircraft's speed through the air mass and therefore forms the magnitude of the air vector.

data.q: After 60 NM an aircraft is 7 NM left of planned track. Its track error is approximately
data.e: At the 60 NM reference distance, 7 NM off represents approximately 7 degrees left.

data.q: After travelling 120 NM from an on-track fix, an aircraft is 8 NM right of track. The track error is
data.e: Sixty multiplied by 8 divided by 120 gives a track error of 4 degrees right.

data.q: An aircraft is 6 NM right of track after 90 NM. What is the approximate track error?
data.e: Sixty multiplied by 6 divided by 90 gives 4 degrees right.

data.q: A fix is 4 NM left of track after 30 NM. The approximate track error is
data.e: Four in 30 scales to eight in 60, so the error is 8 degrees left.

data.q: Planned track is 045 degrees true. After 80 NM the fix is 4 NM left. Track made good is approximately
data.e: The error is 60 multiplied by 4 divided by 80, which is 3 degrees left; 045 minus 3 gives 042 degrees true.

data.q: Planned track is 220 degrees true. A fix 3 NM right after 45 NM gives a track made good of
data.e: The error is 4 degrees right, so track made good is 220 plus 4, or 224 degrees true.

data.q: Using pi as 3.142, the circumference of a circle of radius one unit is
data.e: Circumference is 2 pi r, so a radius of one gives 2 multiplied by 3.142, or 6.284 units.

data.q: One radian is approximately
data.e: One radian equals 360 divided by 2 pi, approximately 57.3 degrees.

data.q: Why is 60 used instead of the exact 57.3 in the pilot rule?
o: It makes the rule exact at every angle
It permits easy mental arithmetic with about 5 percent rounding error
It converts nautical miles to kilometres
data.e: Rounding 57.3 to 60 makes proportional mental arithmetic easy and introduces about 5 percent error.

data.q: At an angle of 10 degrees, the exact opposite side for an adjacent side of 60 units is closest to
data.e: Sixty multiplied by tangent 10 degrees is approximately 10.56 units, closest to 10.6.

data.q: A 5 degree track error continues for 84 NM. The estimated distance off track is
data.e: Distance off is 5 multiplied by 84 divided by 60, which is 7 NM.

data.q: For the track-error triangle, distance gone is measured
o: along track made good to the fix
along planned track to the fix's abeam position
from the fix directly to destination
data.e: Distance gone is the adjacent side measured along planned track from the last on-track point to the present fix's abeam position.

data.q: An aircraft is 4 NM left of track after 30 NM. Its approximate track error is
data.e: Track error is 60 multiplied by 4 divided by 30, which gives 8 degrees left.

data.q: A 78 NM leg has 30 NM gone and a fix 4 NM left of track. What is the closing angle to destination?
data.e: Distance to go is 48 NM, so closing angle is 60 multiplied by 4 divided by 48, or 5 degrees.

data.q: For the same 78 NM leg with a fix 4 NM left after 30 NM, the direct-to-destination heading alteration is
data.e: Track error is 8 degrees and closing angle is 5 degrees, so the aircraft turns 13 degrees right towards track.

data.q: An aircraft is 4 NM left after 30 NM and will regain track after another 30 NM. The first heading alteration is
data.e: With equal outbound and return distances, the double-track-error turn is 2 multiplied by 8 degrees, giving 16 degrees right.

data.q: After the double-track-error correction in the previous question, what turn is made when track is regained?
data.e: At the intercept, an 8 degree left turn removes only the closing angle and leaves the net wind correction.

data.q: On a 95 NM leg, a fix after 35 NM is 7 NM right of track. The heading alteration to fly direct to destination is approximately
data.e: Track error is 12 degrees and closing angle over the remaining 60 NM is 7 degrees, giving a 19 degree turn left.

data.q: A 96 NM leg has 36 NM gone and a fix 3 NM right of track. The direct correction is
data.e: Track error is 5 degrees and closing angle is 3 degrees, so the direct correction is 8 degrees left.

data.q: If a cross-track error developed over 12 minutes and a double-track-error turn is made with unchanged groundspeed, track should be regained after approximately
data.e: The equal-triangle method takes the same time to regain track as the time taken to develop the error, which is 12 minutes.

data.q: A closing angle is 5 degrees on a 78 NM leg with 30 NM gone. The combined correction is
data.e: Combined correction is closing angle multiplied by total distance divided by distance gone: 5 multiplied by 78 divided by 30 equals 13 degrees.

data.q: A fix is one quarter of the way along a leg and the closing angle is 5 degrees. New Track Reference gives a heading alteration of
data.e: Invert one quarter to obtain 4, then multiply by the 5 degree closing angle to obtain 20 degrees.

data.q: An aircraft is 4 NM off track and must regain track 24 NM ahead. The closing angle is
data.e: Closing angle is 60 multiplied by 4 divided by 24, which gives 10 degrees.

data.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes track error from drift?
o: Track error is between planned track and TMG; drift is between heading and track
Track error is between heading and TMG; drift is between planned track and TMG
Both are always the same angle
Drift can be calculated without knowing heading
data.e: Track error compares planned track with track made good, while drift compares heading with a ground track.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: At 2 NM on a 3.5 degree glidepath, the approximate height above the touchdown reference is
data.e: Height is 100 multiplied by 3.5 multiplied by 2, which gives 700 ft.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: At 4 NM on a 2.6 degree glidepath, the approximate height is
data.e: Height is 100 multiplied by 2.6 multiplied by 4, which gives 1040 ft.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: An aircraft is 2 NM from touchdown on a 3 degree path. Its approximate height is
data.e: A 3 degree path changes height by about 300 ft per NM, so at 2 NM the height is 600 ft.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: The required ROD at 120 kt groundspeed on a 3.5 degree path is approximately
data.e: Five times 120, multiplied by 3.5 divided by 3, gives 700 ft/min.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: At 180 kt groundspeed on a 2.6 degree path, the approximate ROD is
data.e: Five times 180, multiplied by 2.6 divided by 3, gives 780 ft/min.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: On a 3 degree path at 150 kt groundspeed, the approximate ROD is
data.e: For a 3 degree path, ROD is about five times groundspeed, giving 750 ft/min.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: Groundspeed reduces from 150 kt to 120 kt on a 3 degree path. To maintain the path, ROD should
data.e: The 30 kt reduction requires a five-times change, so ROD decreases by 150 ft/min.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: On a 2.5 degree path, TAS is 220 kt and headwind is 10 kt. Approximate ROD is
data.e: Groundspeed is 210 kt, so five times 210 multiplied by 2.5 divided by 3 gives 875 ft/min.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: Required inbound QDM is 137 degrees, indicated QDM is 141 degrees and DME range is 90 NM. The aircraft is approximately
data.e: The 4 degree difference at 90 NM gives 4 multiplied by 90 divided by 60, or 6 NM left of centreline.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: A point bearing changes 8 degrees while an aircraft at 120 kt flies for 6 minutes. Approximate range to the point is
data.e: The aircraft flies 12 NM; 12 multiplied by 60 divided by 8 gives a range of 90 NM.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: For a three-degree path, the rapid rate-of-descent factor is
data.e: A 3 degree path is about 300 ft per NM, which gives an ROD of approximately five times groundspeed.

chapter: Other Applications of the 1 in 60 Rule

data.q: A 2 degree angular deviation at a range of 30 NM represents an approximate displacement of
data.e: Displacement is angle multiplied by range divided by 60: 2 multiplied by 30 divided by 60 equals 1 NM.

data.q: Two checkpoints are 20 NM apart and elapsed time is 8 minutes. Measured groundspeed is
data.e: Groundspeed is 20 multiplied by 60 divided by 8, which gives 150 kt.

data.q: An aircraft passes A at 1010 and B, 30 NM farther, at 1027. If 20 NM remains, revised ETA is approximately
data.e: The measured 30 NM took 17 minutes, so the remaining 20 NM takes about 11 minutes and ETA is about 1038.

data.q: An aircraft passes X at 1420 and Y, 30 NM farther, at 1450. If Z is 20 NM beyond Y, ETA at Z is
data.e: The measured groundspeed is 60 kt, so 20 NM takes 20 minutes and ETA is 1510.

data.q: A common planning radius for a circle of uncertainty after 70 NM without a fix is
data.e: Using 10 percent of distance flown gives an uncertainty radius of 7 NM.

data.q: Visual checkpoints are normally selected at intervals of about
data.e: Oxford recommends visual checkpoints at roughly 5 to 10 minute intervals.

data.q: Immediately after setting heading, the navigator should first establish
o: a definite departure point and time
data.e: A definite departure point and departure time provide the origin for the first track and ETA check.

data.q: At a groundspeed of 150 kt, the distance represented by a six-minute chart marker is
data.e: A six-minute marker equals groundspeed divided by 10, so 150 kt gives 15 NM.

data.q: Which sequence best describes the normal in-flight navigation cycle?
data.e: The normal cycle is anticipate, check, correct and record, with heading and ETA revised after a confirmed observation.

data.q: If position is still uncertain when the planned turning-point time arrives, the normal navigation action is to
o: continue straight until a feature appears
data.e: The lost procedure advises turning on the planned ETA rather than continuing indefinitely on the old heading.

data.q: When the expected checkpoint is missing and position is uncertain, the more suitable visual-reading method is
data.e: Ground-to-map starts with observed features and searches the chart for a matching pattern, which suits uncertain position.

data.q: If a safe line feature outside the uncertainty circle is chosen, the aircraft should
o: intercept it and follow it to a definite checkpoint
cross it and continue the same heading
data.e: A line feature can be intercepted and followed until a definite checkpoint allows normal navigation to resume.

data.q: A fix is more than halfway along the leg and the pilot wishes to fly straight to destination. The preferred correction is
o: add track error and closing angle
double track error regardless of distance
data.e: A direct-to-destination correction combines track error with the closing angle for the remaining distance.

data.q: A position line is best described as
o: a line somewhere along which the aircraft is known to be at a stated time
the line joining two planned waypoints
data.e: A position line is a line somewhere along which the aircraft is known to be at the observation time.

data.q: Fixes at 1700 and 1730 are 100 NM apart. The measured groundspeed is
data.e: One hundred nautical miles in 30 minutes is 200 kt.

data.q: A QDM of 330 degrees magnetic is converted to its QDR by taking the reciprocal. The QDR is
data.e: The reciprocal of QDM 330 M is QDR 150 M.

data.q: When plotting a VOR radial after magnetic-to-true conversion, the applicable variation is normally at
data.e: A VOR bearing is referenced and measured at the ground station, so station variation is used.

data.q: An aircraft heads 315 M where aircraft variation is 9 degrees west. An NDB bears 207 relative. The true bearing to plot FROM the NDB is
data.e: True heading is 306 T; adding relative 207 gives 153 T TO, whose reciprocal is 333 T FROM the NDB.

data.q: Two DME range circles normally create
data.e: Two circles normally intersect at two possible positions, so DR position, heading or range trend resolves the ambiguity.

data.q: At 120 kt, a position line observed 10 minutes earlier is transferred along track by
data.e: Transfer distance is 120 multiplied by 10 divided by 60, which equals 20 NM.

data.q: To construct a running fix, the earlier position line is
o: moved parallel to itself by estimated ground movement
data.e: The complete earlier line is moved parallel to itself in track direction by the estimated distance travelled.

data.q: The size of a cocked hat primarily indicates
o: agreement and probable accuracy of the position lines
data.e: A smaller cocked hat shows closer agreement of the plotted lines, though common systematic error can still shift them.

data.q: On an air and ground plot for the same interval, the vector from air position to ground position represents
data.e: The difference between air position and simultaneous ground position is the displacement caused by wind.

data.q: On a Lambert chart, an aircraft-measured ADF bearing is most accurately plotted from
o: a line through the NDB parallel to the aircraft meridian
data.e: A false meridian through the NDB, parallel to the aircraft meridian, automatically allows for chart convergence.

data.q: To lose 23,000 ft over 65 NM at a groundspeed of 240 kt, the approximate rate of descent is
data.e: The flight covers 65 NM in 16.25 minutes, and 23,000 divided by 16.25 is about 1415 ft per minute.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: Two aircraft 460 NM apart fly directly towards each other at groundspeeds of 250 kt and 210 kt. Their closing speed is
data.e: For head-on motion the groundspeeds add, giving a closing speed of 460 kt.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: An aircraft at 220 kt is 80 NM behind traffic at 180 kt on the same track. Time to overtake is
data.e: Relative closing speed is 40 kt, so 80 NM divided by 40 kt gives 2 hours.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: A beacon changes from relative bearing 270 to 225 in 3 minutes while GS is 180 kt. For the stated isosceles geometry, closest approach is
data.e: The aircraft travels 9 NM in 3 minutes, and the 45-degree isosceles geometry makes closest approach also 9 NM.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: In exact triangle-of-velocities geometry, zero head or tail component occurs when wind is at right angles to
o: the bisector between heading and track
data.e: Strictly, the wind must be perpendicular to the bisector between heading and track for zero along-track component.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: Safe endurance used in a PNR calculation is
o: time available after protected reserves are excluded
all fuel on board including unusable fuel
data.e: Safe endurance is the time available for the defined outbound and return operation after protected reserves and unusable fuel are removed.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: Safe endurance is 8 hours, outbound GS 450 kt and homebound GS 350 kt. Time to PNR is
data.e: PNR time is 8 multiplied by 350 divided by 800, which equals 3.5 hours.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: Which expression gives PNR distance from base when E is safe endurance, O outbound GS and H homebound GS?
o: E x O x H / (O + H)
data.e: PNR distance equals E multiplied by O multiplied by H, divided by O plus H.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: With E 10 hours, outbound GS 300 kt and homebound GS 500 kt, PNR distance is
data.e: PNR time is 10 x 500 / 800 = 6.25 hours, and 6.25 x 300 gives 1875 NM.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: Available decision fuel is 3000 kg. Outbound flow is 500 kg/h at 400 kt and homebound flow 400 kg/h at 500 kt. Fuel-limited PNR distance is about
data.e: Distance is 3000 divided by (500/400 + 400/500), which is approximately 1463 NM.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: For a 2400 NM route with outbound GS 480 kt and homebound GS 320 kt, CP distance from base is
data.e: CP distance is 2400 multiplied by 320 divided by 800, giving 960 NM.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: An along-track wind moves the critical point towards
o: the route midpoint in every case
data.e: The critical point shifts towards the upwind endpoint because travel is slower in that direction.

chapter: Navigation Problems: Relative Velocity, PNR and CP

data.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes CP from PNR?
o: CP uses route distance and both groundspeeds, while PNR uses safe endurance
PNR is always the route midpoint
CP is determined only by fuel flow
data.e: CP is an equal-time point based on route distance and groundspeeds; PNR is an endurance or fuel-limited return point.
